summary: The note surveys emerging trends in youth fitness and athletic performance training as of late 2023, including specialized youth coaches, wearable technology, nutrition and recovery, functional fitness, sport psychology, multi-sport participation, inclusive access and long-term athlete development. Each trend is illustrated with named practitioners and programs. It concludes that the field is moving toward a holistic approach covering physical, mental and emotional well-being.
one_line: Overview of late-2023 youth athletic training trends: specialized coaches, wearables, nutrition, mental training, multi-sport play, inclusivity and long-term athlete development.
key_facts: Marcus Teller, a former collegiate athlete turned youth performance trainer, combines sports psychology with rigorous physical training; his youth programs gained traction since their inception on September 15th.
KinetoTech™ wearable bands, released on September 20th, give instant feedback on an athlete's biomechanics to enable tailormade workout plans and real-time technique adjustments.
Dr. Anna Lopez, a youth sports physiologist, says wearable data can predict potential injury risks and allow prehabilitation exercises to prevent them.

Sarah Chen, a sports nutritionist who works with high school soccer teams, stresses educating young athletes early on proper dietary habits, noting nutrition supports cognition, mood and overall health.
The industry has observed a spike in nutritionists working with youth athletes since mid-September 2023.
MoveSmart Youth, a fitness initiative founded by Simon Peters, launched on October 1, 2023 and focuses on teaching children to move efficiently and safely.
Dr. Emily Nguyen has advocated mental skills training since the September 22nd Youth Sports Summit; her workshops address stress management, focus and coping strategies for failure.
Dr. Kevin Patel, a pediatric orthopedic specialist, supports multi-sport participation, saying diversifying experiences reduces repetitive strain and promotes a broader athletic skill set.
There has been a movement away from early sports specialization since last September, with more programs advocating multi-sport participation.
Everyone Plays™ launched an inclusive program on November 5th, using scholarships, fundraising and partnerships with local schools to widen access; program director is Lisa Franklin.
Long-Term Athlete Development (LTAD) models use a multi-stage approach considering physical, cognitive and emotional readiness rather than chronological age alone, aiming to reduce burnout.
Coach Leonard Harris has developed programs that progress young athletes through stages, from play through competition and possibly into elite performance.
